content.text:
I've saved the revised F10 in `finding.json` and marked the challenge as accepted. The main pattern holds and some of the evidence for it is stronger now, but the cost figure drops from $84,943/yr to $69,682/yr (q393). I ran no new queries, because I found nothing in the challenge to dispute; every number in the file comes from my queries or the challenger's.

**What changed:**
- **Cost:** all 137 jobs with "wrong revision" scrap were scrapped whole, none shipped, and every one was remade on the same order line (q388). So the selling price was billed on the remake, and the real loss is the cost of the scrapped run. The new figure is $69,682/yr over 10 years (q387, q393):
  - $39,195 a year of scrap cost: material $331,519 plus labour $60,427 (2,420 hours at the average pay rate of $24.97, without overheads).
  - $30,487 a year of credits for parts returned as not fitting, wrong dimensions or nonconforming ($304,873 over the 10 years).
  - The credits are an upper bound on what could be avoided; the labour is roughly a floor. Remaking returned parts isn't counted.
- **Scrap and returns are different jobs:** none of the scrapped jobs has a return (q388). The finding now says scrap is what the shop caught itself and returns are what got out to customers, not the same events.
- **The ECO gap is better supported:** I added the challenger's tests, and the gap survives all of them:
  - Jobs where a new revision arrived mid-job with no engineering change order (ECO) logged against them have far more wrong-revision scrap than those with one. That holds within the same customers (40.3% vs 0.7%) and the same parts (48.1% vs 1.1%) (q394).
  - It holds whether or not engineering released the new revision before the job finished, and job lengths are similar (q380).
  - An ECO on another job for the same part didn't protect a job: 26 of those 49 jobs still had the scrap (q381). So the recommended check is now explicitly per job.
- **The count of jobs released on an old revision depends on the definition:** it's 82 if you use the date a revision was received and 136 if you use the date it was logged (q392). Neither matches the 158 from the earlier query q26. I moved that to "could not tell" and made the combined group of at-risk jobs the headline.
- **ECO and cause:** I adopted the challenger's caveat. An ECO may simply record that someone caught the change in time, rather than being what prevents the scrap. Telling these apart would need timestamps on when job packets were updated and a revision check at first-article inspection.

Confidence stays medium. "Wrong revision" is a code staff enter themselves, and the records don't show which revision was actually machined.
